questions.q: What is the SI unit of speed, and which standard unit is commonly used for long-distance vehicle travel in India?
questions.a: The SI unit of speed is metres per second ($\text{m/s}$), while kilometres per hour ($\text{km/h}$) is commonly used for vehicle travel. A wrong answer shows confusion between fundamental physical quantities or mistaking practical units for official SI standards.

questions.q: Why do we multiply a speed given in $\text{km/h}$ by $\frac{5}{18}$ to convert it into $\text{m/s}$? Explain the origin of this fraction.
questions.a: We multiply by $\frac{5}{18}$ because $1\text{ km} = 1000\text{ m}$ and $1\text{ hour} = 3600\text{ s}$, so $\frac{1000}{3600}$ simplifies by dividing numerator and denominator by $200$ to get $\frac{5}{18}$. A wrong answer indicates rote memorization of the trick without understanding dimensional scaling of units.

questions.q: Convert a speed of $72\text{ km/h}$ into metres per second ($\text{m/s}$).
questions.a: $20\text{ m/s}$. Working: Multiply $72$ by $\frac{5}{18}$. We get $72 \times \frac{5}{18} = 4 \times 5 = 20\text{ m/s}$. A wrong answer reveals an error in simplifying fractions or mistakenly multiplying by $\frac{18}{5}$ instead.

questions.q: A student states that $36\text{ km/h}$ is equivalent to $36\text{ m/s}$ because the numerical value remains the same. Evaluate this statement and point out the error.
questions.a: The statement is incorrect because units change the magnitude relationship. $36\text{ km/h}$ equals $36 \times \frac{5}{18} = 10\text{ m/s}$, not $36\text{ m/s}$. A wrong answer indicates a lack of conceptual understanding of what units represent in physical measurement.

questions.q: Design a short word problem involving an Indian express train where converting units is essential to determine if it beats a highway bus travelling at $60\text{ km/h}$.
questions.a: A good problem states the train's speed in $\text{m/s}$ (e.g., $20\text{ m/s}$) and asks students to convert it to $\text{km/h}$ ($72\text{ km/h}$) to compare with the bus ($60\text{ km/h}$) and conclude the train is faster. A poor problem lacks realistic numbers or fails to require unit conversion.

questions.q: Create a two-line "conversion card" for travellers that converts any speed from $\text{km/h}$ into $\text{m/s}$ in one step and back again, and demonstrate your card on $90\text{ km/h}$.
questions.a: A good card states both multipliers — "$\text{km/h} \rightarrow \text{m/s}$: multiply by $\frac{5}{18}$" and "$\text{m/s} \rightarrow \text{km/h}$: multiply by $\frac{18}{5}$" — with the check that the $\text{m/s}$ value must always be the smaller number. Applied to $90\text{ km/h}$ it gives $90 \times \frac{5}{18} = 25\text{ m/s}$, which is indeed smaller. A poor card memorises only one fraction with no size check, so it fails the moment the direction of conversion flips.

questions.q: Fill in the blank: Imagine riding a bicycle down an Indian village road where the speedometer or milestone markers indicate distance in ______ and time in hours, while a school laboratory stopwatch measures time in seconds.

Fill in the blank: Imagine riding a bicycle down an Indian village road where the ______ or milestone markers indicate distance in kilometres and time in hours, while a school laboratory stopwatch measures time in seconds.
